tool.name: Amazon DynamoDB
tool.tagline: AWS's serverless key-value and document database with single-digit-ms latency
tool.description: Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database on AWS that stores items by key and scales to virtually any traffic with predictable low latency and no servers to run. It powers shopping carts, sessions, game state, IoT and many serverless backends. Learning it means learning to design data around access patterns instead of joins.

concepts.name: What DynamoDB is
concepts.summary: A fully managed key-value and document database: tables of items looked up by key, with no servers and near-unlimited scale.
concepts.why: Knowing its strengths and limits up front tells you when DynamoDB is the right store and how differently you must think about data.
concepts.body:
**DynamoDB** is AWS's serverless NoSQL database. You create a **table**, write **items** (records, like rows) into it, and read them back by key with single-digit-millisecond latency, whether the table holds a megabyte or a hundred terabytes. There are no instances to size, patch or fail over: AWS replicates every table across three Availability Zones and scales it for you.

Each item is a set of **attributes** (name/value pairs). Apart from the key attributes, items in one table can have completely different attributes; there is no fixed schema. An item can be up to 400 KB.

The trade-off is in querying. There are no joins, no ad-hoc SQL across the whole table and no aggregations. Efficient reads always go through a key: fetch one item by its primary key, or query a group of items that share a partition key. Scanning the whole table works but is slow and expensive.

So DynamoDB fits workloads with **known access patterns** at high or spiky scale: user profiles, shopping carts, sessions, game state, device data, serverless APIs. It fits poorly when you need flexible analytical queries; you would export the data to S3 and query it with Athena, or use a relational database instead.

You talk to it with the AWS SDKs (in Python, `boto3`), the AWS CLI or the console.
takeaways: Tables hold schemaless items; only the key attributes are required
Fast reads always go through the primary key or an index
No joins or ad-hoc queries: design for known access patterns
Fully managed, multi-AZ and serverless
pitfalls: Choosing DynamoDB for a reporting workload that needs arbitrary filters and joins.

options: Ad-hoc analytical queries joining many tables
A shopping cart looked up by user id at very high traffic
Full-text search across product descriptions
Monthly reports with arbitrary GROUP BY
quiz.explain: Key-based lookups with known access patterns at scale are exactly what DynamoDB is built for.

concepts.name: Partition keys and sort keys
concepts.summary: The primary key is a partition key alone or a partition key plus sort key; it decides where items live and how you can query them.
concepts.why: Choosing the key is the most important design decision for any DynamoDB table and cannot be changed later.
concepts.body:
Every table has a **primary key**, declared at creation and immutable afterwards. It comes in two forms:

- **Simple key**: a single **partition key** (also called hash key). Each value identifies exactly one item, e.g. `user_id`.
- **Composite key**: a partition key plus a **sort key** (range key). Many items can share a partition key as long as their sort keys differ, e.g. `customer_id` + `order_id`.

DynamoDB hashes the partition key to decide which physical **partition** (storage node) holds the item. All items with the same partition key are stored together, sorted by sort key; this group is called an **item collection**.

That layout explains the query rules. You can:

- get one item if you know its full primary key
- query one item collection: all items for a partition key, optionally narrowed with a sort key condition like `=`, `<`, `between` or `begins_with`, returned in sort-key order

You cannot efficiently ask "all orders over 100 dollars" across customers without an index, because those items live in different partitions.

Good partition keys have many distinct values that are accessed fairly evenly (user ids, device ids). Sort keys are often made sortable on purpose, such as ISO dates (`2025-03-01#A17`) or prefixes (`ORDER#...`), so that range queries return useful slices.
concepts.code:
# Table "Orders": partition key customer_id, sort key order_id
#
# customer_id | order_id         | total | status
# ------------+------------------+-------+---------
# c1          | 2025-01-09#A11   | 20    | SHIPPED   <- item collection "c1",
# c1          | 2025-03-01#A17   | 35    | PENDING      stored together, sorted
# c1          | 2025-03-14#A20   | 12    | PENDING      by order_id
# c2          | 2025-02-02#B03   | 99    | SHIPPED   <- lives on another partition
#
# Efficient:  get c1 / 2025-03-01#A17
#             all orders of c1 in March 2025:
#               customer_id = "c1" AND begins_with(order_id, "2025-03")
# Not efficient without an index: all PENDING orders of every customer
takeaways: Primary key = partition key, or partition key + sort key
The partition key's hash decides placement; items sharing it form a sorted item collection
Queries target one partition key and can filter/sort on the sort key
Design sort keys (dates, prefixes) so range queries return useful slices
pitfalls: Using a low-cardinality partition key such as status or country, which concentrates traffic on a few partitions.

quiz.q: A table's key is (customer_id, order_id). Which request can DynamoDB serve efficiently?
options: All orders for customer c1 whose order_id begins with 2025-03
All orders with total > 50 across all customers
The 10 most expensive orders overall
All customers whose name starts with A
quiz.explain: It targets one partition key and uses a sort key condition, so it reads a single sorted item collection.

concepts.name: Attribute types and boto3
concepts.summary: DynamoDB's attribute types (string, number, binary, boolean, null, map, list, sets) and how boto3 maps them to Python.
concepts.why: Type mismatches, especially floats and Decimals, are the first errors every Python developer hits.
concepts.body:
DynamoDB attribute values have one of these types:

- scalars: **S** (string), **N** (number), **B** (binary), **BOOL**, **NULL**
- documents: **M** (map, a nested object) and **L** (list, any mix of types)
- sets: **SS**, **NS**, **BS** (unique strings, numbers or binaries; never empty)

Key attributes must be S, N or B. Numbers are sent as strings and stored with up to 38 digits of precision, so they are exact decimals rather than floats.

boto3 has two interfaces. The low-level **client** speaks the wire format, where every value is wrapped with its type: `{"total": {"N": "35"}}`. The higher-level **resource** (`boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table(...)`) converts automatically between Python and DynamoDB types:

- `str` to S, `bool` to BOOL, `None` to NULL, `dict` to M, `list` to L, `set` to a set type, `bytes` to B
- numbers come back as `decimal.Decimal`, and you must send `int` or `Decimal`, **not `float`**

Passing a float raises `TypeError: Float types are not supported`. Convert with `Decimal(str(x))`, or keep money in integer cents. When returning items as JSON from an API, convert Decimals back (e.g. a custom `default=` in `json.dumps`).

The resource interface is the most readable for scripts; the client offers every API and is required for some newer features.
concepts.code:
from decimal import Decimal
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")

table.put_item(Item={
    "customer_id": "c1", "order_id": "2025-03-01#A17",
    "total": Decimal("35.90"),          # not 35.90 (float raises TypeError)
    "paid": True,
    "items": [{"sku": "pen", "qty": 2}],  # list of maps
    "tags": {"gift", "express"},          # string set
})
item = table.get_item(Key={"customer_id": "c1", "order_id": "2025-03-01#A17"})["Item"]
print(item["total"], type(item["total"]).__name__)   # 35.90 Decimal
print(item["items"][0]["qty"])                       # 2  (also a Decimal)
takeaways: Types: S, N, B, BOOL, NULL, M, L and the sets SS/NS/BS
Key attributes must be string, number or binary
The boto3 resource maps Python types automatically; numbers come back as Decimal
Never send floats: use Decimal or integers
pitfalls: Passing a Python float to put_item and getting 'Float types are not supported'.

quiz.q: Why does boto3's Table.put_item reject the value 9.99 (a float)?
options: DynamoDB cannot store fractional numbers
Only key attributes can be numbers
Numbers must be sent as strings by the caller
Floats would lose precision, so boto3 requires Decimal or int
quiz.explain: DynamoDB numbers are exact decimals, so boto3 refuses inexact binary floats and asks for Decimal.

concepts.name: Creating tables and DynamoDB Local
concepts.summary: Create a table with boto3, choose on-demand billing, wait until it is active, and develop against DynamoDB Local.
concepts.why: You need a table to do anything, and a local copy of DynamoDB makes development fast, free and safe.
concepts.body:
`create_table` needs only the key schema and the types of the key attributes; other attributes are never declared.

- `KeySchema`: the partition key (`HASH`) and optional sort key (`RANGE`)
- `AttributeDefinitions`: name and type (`S`, `N`, `B`) for every key attribute, including index keys, and nothing else
- `BillingMode`: `PAY_PER_REQUEST` (on-demand: pay per request, no capacity planning) or `PROVISIONED` with `ProvisionedThroughput`

Creation is asynchronous: the table starts in `CREATING` state, so wait with `table.wait_until_exists()` or a waiter before writing.

For development, run **DynamoDB Local**, a downloadable version of DynamoDB (a Java jar or the `amazon/dynamodb-local` Docker image), and point the SDK at it with `endpoint_url="http://localhost:8000"`. It accepts any credentials and region. For unit tests in Python, the `moto` library mocks DynamoDB in-process.

Infrastructure as code (CloudFormation, CDK, Terraform) is how real tables are created in production, with the same settings expressed declaratively. Enable **point-in-time recovery** and **deletion protection** on any table that matters; both are a single setting.

Table names are unique per account and region.
concepts.code:
import boto3

# docker run -p 8000:8000 amazon/dynamodb-local
ddb = boto3.resource("dynamodb", endpoint_url="http://localhost:8000",
                     region_name="us-east-1",
                     aws_access_key_id="x", aws_secret_access_key="x")

table = ddb.create_table(
    TableName="Orders",
    KeySchema=[{"AttributeName": "customer_id", "KeyType": "HASH"},
               {"AttributeName": "order_id", "KeyType": "RANGE"}],
    AttributeDefinitions=[{"AttributeName": "customer_id", "AttributeType": "S"},
                          {"AttributeName": "order_id", "AttributeType": "S"}],
    BillingMode="PAY_PER_REQUEST",
)
table.wait_until_exists()
print(table.table_status)        # ACTIVE
print(table.key_schema[0])       # {'AttributeName': 'customer_id', 'KeyType': 'HASH'}
takeaways: Declare only key attributes in AttributeDefinitions
`PAY_PER_REQUEST` (on-demand) avoids capacity planning
Wait for ACTIVE before using a new table
Develop against DynamoDB Local or moto, not production
pitfalls: Listing non-key attributes in AttributeDefinitions, which makes create_table fail with a validation error.

quiz.q: Which attributes go into AttributeDefinitions when creating a table?
options: Every attribute your items will have
Only the partition key
Only attributes used as keys of the table or its indexes
None; DynamoDB infers them
quiz.explain: DynamoDB is schemaless except for keys, so only key attributes (table and index) are declared.

concepts.name: Put, get, update and delete items
concepts.summary: The four single-item operations: put_item, get_item, update_item and delete_item, all addressed by the full primary key.
concepts.why: Single-item operations by key are the bread and butter of every DynamoDB application.
concepts.body:
All single-item operations take the **full primary key** (partition key, plus sort key if the table has one).

- `put_item(Item=...)` writes a whole item. If an item with that key exists, it is **replaced entirely**: attributes you did not include are gone.
- `get_item(Key=...)` reads one item. The response has an `Item` field only if it exists, so use `resp.get("Item")`. Reads are eventually consistent by default; pass `ConsistentRead=True` for a strongly consistent read.
- `update_item(Key=..., UpdateExpression=...)` changes some attributes in place and creates the item if it does not exist. `ReturnValues="ALL_NEW"` returns the updated item, saving a separate read.
- `delete_item(Key=...)` removes an item; deleting a missing item is not an error.

Each write is atomic for that item, and all four accept a `ConditionExpression` (covered later) to make the operation happen only if the item is in an expected state.

Remember the asymmetry: put replaces, update merges. Use `update_item` for counters, status changes and partial edits, and `put_item` when you own the whole item.

`ProjectionExpression` on `get_item` returns only the attributes you list, which saves bandwidth but not read capacity: you pay for the full item size.
concepts.code:
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
key = {"customer_id": "c1", "order_id": "2025-03-01#A17"}

table.put_item(Item={**key, "total": 35, "status": "PENDING"})

resp = table.update_item(
    Key=key,
    UpdateExpression="SET #s = :s",
    ExpressionAttributeNames={"#s": "status"},      # status is a reserved word
    ExpressionAttributeValues={":s": "SHIPPED"},
    ReturnValues="ALL_NEW",
)
print(resp["Attributes"]["status"])                 # SHIPPED

print(table.get_item(Key=key)["Item"]["total"])     # 35
table.delete_item(Key=key)
print(table.get_item(Key=key).get("Item"))          # None
takeaways: Every single-item call needs the full primary key
put_item replaces the whole item; update_item modifies attributes and upserts
get_item returns no Item key when the item does not exist
Use ReturnValues to get the new or old item back from a write
pitfalls: Using put_item to change one attribute and accidentally wiping all the others.

quiz.q: An item has attributes a, b and c. You call put_item with the same key and only attribute a. What is stored?
options: a, b and c with a updated
Only a (plus the key)
An error is raised because b and c are missing
Two items with the same key
quiz.explain: put_item replaces the whole item, so attributes not supplied are removed.

concepts.name: Query an item collection
concepts.summary: Query all items for one partition key, narrow with sort key conditions, sort ascending or descending and limit results.
concepts.why: Query is the efficient way to read many items and the operation most access patterns are built on.
concepts.body:
`Query` reads items from **one** item collection: you must give an equality condition on the partition key, and you may add one condition on the sort key: `=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `between`, or `begins_with`.

With the boto3 resource you build these with `boto3.dynamodb.conditions.Key`:

```python
Key("customer_id").eq("c1") & Key("order_id").begins_with("2025-03")
```

Results come back **sorted by sort key**, ascending by default; `ScanIndexForward=False` returns them descending, which together with `Limit=1` is the idiom for "latest item" (most recent order, last reading of a sensor).

Because a query reads one contiguous range on one partition, its cost depends only on the size of the items it reads, not on the size of the table. That is why designs that turn access patterns into queries scale so well.

A query returns at most 1 MB of data per call. If there is more, the response contains `LastEvaluatedKey` and you must call again with `ExclusiveStartKey` (see pagination).

A `FilterExpression` can drop items after they are read, but you still pay for reading them; filters are a convenience, not a substitute for good keys.
concepts.code:
import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
for oid in ["2025-01-09#A11", "2025-03-01#A17", "2025-03-14#A20"]:
    table.put_item(Item={"customer_id": "c1", "order_id": oid})

march = table.query(
    KeyConditionExpression=Key("customer_id").eq("c1")
                           & Key("order_id").begins_with("2025-03"))
print([i["order_id"] for i in march["Items"]])
# ['2025-03-01#A17', '2025-03-14#A20']

latest = table.query(KeyConditionExpression=Key("customer_id").eq("c1"),
                     ScanIndexForward=False, Limit=1)
print(latest["Items"][0]["order_id"])   # 2025-03-14#A20
takeaways: Query needs partition key equality and allows one sort key condition
Results are ordered by sort key; ScanIndexForward=False reverses
Cost depends on items read, not table size
FilterExpression runs after the read and does not reduce cost
pitfalls: Expecting a FilterExpression to make a query cheaper; you pay for everything read before filtering.

quiz.q: How do you get the most recent order for c1 when order_id starts with an ISO date?
options: Query c1 with ScanIndexForward=False and Limit=1
Scan the table and sort in Python
Query c1 with Limit=1 (ascending)
get_item with only the partition key
quiz.explain: Descending order by sort key plus a limit of one returns the item with the largest order_id.

concepts.name: Scan and pagination
concepts.summary: Read a whole table with Scan, page through any result with LastEvaluatedKey, and use parallel scans when you must.
concepts.why: Every listing needs pagination, and knowing why Scan is expensive keeps it out of request paths.
concepts.body:
`Scan` reads **every item** in a table or index, optionally dropping some with a `FilterExpression`. It consumes read capacity for everything it touches, so on a large table it is slow and costly. Use it for exports, migrations and admin jobs, not on a user's request path.

Both Query and Scan return at most **1 MB** per call (or `Limit` items read). When more data remains, the response includes `LastEvaluatedKey`; pass it as `ExclusiveStartKey` in the next call. Keep going until the key is absent. Note that `Limit` caps items **evaluated**, before filtering, so a page can come back with fewer items than `Limit`, or even zero, while more pages remain.

For APIs, return `LastEvaluatedKey` (serialized, often base64 JSON) to the client as an opaque cursor. DynamoDB has no offset pagination: you cannot jump to page 7.

For big jobs, a **parallel scan** splits the table into `TotalSegments` and lets workers each scan one `Segment` concurrently. For full exports to analytics, the managed **Export to S3** feature is better still: it reads from a point-in-time backup and consumes no table capacity.

The low-level client also offers paginators (`client.get_paginator("query")`) that loop for you.
concepts.code:
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")

def scan_all(table, **kwargs):
    """Yield every item, following LastEvaluatedKey page by page."""
    while True:
        page = table.scan(**kwargs)
        yield from page["Items"]
        if "LastEvaluatedKey" not in page:
            return
        kwargs["ExclusiveStartKey"] = page["LastEvaluatedKey"]

with table.batch_writer() as bw:
    for n in range(250):
        bw.put_item(Item={"customer_id": f"c{n % 7}", "order_id": f"o{n:04}"})

print(sum(1 for _ in scan_all(table, Limit=40)))   # 250  (7 pages of up to 40)
takeaways: Scan reads and bills for every item, filters or not
Pages are at most 1 MB; follow LastEvaluatedKey until it is missing
Limit counts items evaluated before filtering
Prefer Export to S3 or parallel scans for whole-table jobs
pitfalls: Treating an empty page as the end of results while LastEvaluatedKey is still present.

quiz.q: A Scan with Limit=100 and a FilterExpression returns 0 items and a LastEvaluatedKey. What does that mean?
options: The table is empty
The scan failed and must be retried
The filter is invalid
100 items were evaluated, none matched, and more items remain
quiz.explain: Limit applies before filtering; the presence of LastEvaluatedKey means there are more pages to read.

concepts.name: Update, condition and projection expressions
concepts.summary: Write UpdateExpressions with SET, REMOVE, ADD and DELETE, plus placeholders for names and values.
concepts.why: Expressions are how you modify, protect and trim items, and the syntax trips everyone up at first.
concepts.body:
DynamoDB uses small expression languages instead of SQL.

An **UpdateExpression** has up to four clauses, each used once:

- `SET a = :v, b = b + :one, c = if_not_exists(c, :zero), l = list_append(l, :new)`
- `REMOVE attr, list[0]` deletes attributes or list elements
- `ADD counter :n` increments a number (creating it at 0 if missing) or adds to a set
- `DELETE tags :old` removes elements from a set

Nested paths use dots and indexes: `address.city`, `items[2].qty`.

Values are never written inline. Use **placeholders**: `:name` for values in `ExpressionAttributeValues`, and `#name` in `ExpressionAttributeNames` for attribute names that are reserved words (`status`, `name`, `date`, `count` and hundreds more) or contain special characters.

A **ConditionExpression** uses comparisons, `AND/OR/NOT`, `BETWEEN`, `IN`, and functions like `attribute_exists(a)`, `attribute_not_exists(a)`, `begins_with`, `contains`, `size`. A **ProjectionExpression** lists attributes to return. In boto3 the resource layer lets you write conditions with `Attr("x").gt(1)` objects instead of strings.

`ADD` and `SET x = x + :n` are atomic increments: safe under concurrency without reading first.
concepts.code:
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
key = {"customer_id": "c9", "order_id": "o1"}
table.put_item(Item={**key, "tags": {"new"}, "notes": "fragile"})

r = table.update_item(
    Key=key,
    UpdateExpression=("SET #st = :st, page_views = if_not_exists(page_views, :zero) + :one "
                      "REMOVE notes ADD tags :t"),
    ExpressionAttributeNames={"#st": "status"},
    ExpressionAttributeValues={":st": "PAID", ":zero": 0, ":one": 1, ":t": {"vip"}},
    ReturnValues="ALL_NEW",
)
item = r["Attributes"]
print(item["status"], item["page_views"], sorted(item["tags"]), "notes" in item)
# PAID 1 ['new', 'vip'] False
takeaways: UpdateExpression clauses: SET, REMOVE, ADD, DELETE
Values go in `:placeholders`, reserved or odd names in `#placeholders`
`if_not_exists` and `ADD` give safe defaults and atomic counters
Conditions use functions like attribute_exists and begins_with
pitfalls: Writing an attribute called status or name directly in an expression and getting a reserved-word ValidationException.

quiz.q: Two clients call update_item with 'ADD views :one' on the same item at the same moment. What is the final increase?
options: 1, because one update overwrites the other
It depends on which client reads first
2, because ADD is applied atomically on the server
An error, because concurrent updates conflict
quiz.explain: The increment happens inside DynamoDB per request, so both are applied without a read-modify-write race.

concepts.name: Conditional writes and optimistic locking
concepts.summary: Make writes succeed only if the item is in an expected state: create-only puts, guarded updates and version numbers.
concepts.why: Conditions are DynamoDB's tool for correctness under concurrency, without locks or transactions.
concepts.body:
Any put, update or delete can carry a `ConditionExpression`. DynamoDB evaluates it against the current item **atomically** with the write; if it is false, nothing is written and the call fails with `ConditionalCheckFailedException`.

Common patterns:

- **Create only if new**: `put_item(..., ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(customer_id)")`. Checking the partition key attribute is the idiom for "no item with this key exists".
- **Guard a state transition**: `update_item(... SET #s = :shipped, ConditionExpression="#s = :paid")` so an order can only ship once it is paid.
- **Never go negative**: `SET stock = stock - :n` with condition `stock >= :n`.
- **Optimistic locking**: store a `version` number. Read the item, change it, then write with `version = :read_version` in the condition and `version = version + 1` in the update. If someone else wrote in between, your write fails and you re-read and retry.

Catch the error via `client.exceptions.ConditionalCheckFailedException` (the resource exposes it as `table.meta.client.exceptions...`). Add `ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure="ALL_OLD"` to receive the current item in the error and avoid another read.

A failed condition still consumes write capacity.
concepts.code:
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
errors = table.meta.client.exceptions
key = {"customer_id": "c5", "order_id": "o1"}

table.put_item(Item={**key, "stock": 3, "version": 1},
               ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(customer_id)")
try:  # same key again: refused
    table.put_item(Item={**key, "stock": 0, "version": 1},
                   ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(customer_id)")
except errors.ConditionalCheckFailedException:
    print("already exists")                    # already exists

def take(n, seen_version):
    table.update_item(Key=key,
        UpdateExpression="SET stock = stock - :n, version = version + :one",
        ConditionExpression="stock >= :n AND version = :v",
        ExpressionAttributeValues={":n": n, ":one": 1, ":v": seen_version})

take(2, 1)                                     # ok: stock 1, version 2
try:
    take(1, 1)                                 # stale version
except errors.ConditionalCheckFailedException:
    print("conflict, re-read and retry")       # conflict, re-read and retry
takeaways: Conditions are checked atomically with the write
`attribute_not_exists(pk)` means create-only
Version attributes implement optimistic locking
Handle ConditionalCheckFailedException as an expected outcome
pitfalls: Reading an item, checking a value in application code and then writing without a condition: another writer can slip in between.

quiz.q: What happens when a conditional update's condition is false?
options: The update is applied and a warning returned
Nothing is written and ConditionalCheckFailedException is raised
DynamoDB waits until the condition becomes true
The item is deleted
quiz.explain: A false condition aborts the write and raises an exception the caller handles.

concepts.name: Global and local secondary indexes
concepts.summary: Add GSIs and LSIs to query by other attributes, choose projections, and understand their consistency and limits.
concepts.why: Most real tables need more than one access pattern, and indexes are how DynamoDB serves them.
concepts.body:
A **secondary index** is an alternate key over the same items, maintained automatically, that you `Query` (or `Scan`) with `IndexName=...`.

A **global secondary index (GSI)** has its own partition key and optional sort key, any attributes you like. It is effectively a separate table that DynamoDB keeps in sync **asynchronously**:

- reads are **eventually consistent** only
- it has its own capacity (on provisioned tables, under-provisioning a GSI throttles writes to the base table)
- you can add or delete it at any time; default limit 20 per table
- keys do not have to be unique in an index

A **local secondary index (LSI)** keeps the table's partition key but uses a different sort key. It must be created with the table, supports strongly consistent reads, and imposes a 10 GB limit per item collection. Up to 5 per table. Prefer GSIs unless you need strong consistency on the alternate sort order.

**Projections** decide which attributes are copied into the index: `KEYS_ONLY`, `INCLUDE` (a list) or `ALL`. Querying an index only returns projected attributes; wider projections cost more storage and write capacity.

Only items that have the index key attributes appear in the index. That is a feature: it enables **sparse indexes**, covered later.
concepts.code:
import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key

client = boto3.client("dynamodb")
client.update_table(                      # add a GSI to an existing table
    TableName="Orders",
    AttributeDefinitions=[{"AttributeName": "status", "AttributeType": "S"},
                          {"AttributeName": "order_id", "AttributeType": "S"}],
    GlobalSecondaryIndexUpdates=[{"Create": {
        "IndexName": "status-index",
        "KeySchema": [{"AttributeName": "status", "KeyType": "HASH"},
                      {"AttributeName": "order_id", "KeyType": "RANGE"}],
        "Projection": {"ProjectionType": "INCLUDE", "NonKeyAttributes": ["total"]},
    }}],
)
# ...once the index is ACTIVE:
table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
pending = table.query(IndexName="status-index",
                      KeyConditionExpression=Key("status").eq("PENDING"))
print([i["order_id"] for i in pending["Items"]])
takeaways: GSIs: any key, added anytime, eventually consistent, own capacity
LSIs: same partition key, other sort key, created with the table, 10 GB per collection
Projections control which attributes an index returns
Items without the index key are simply absent from the index
pitfalls: Reading from a GSI immediately after a write and expecting to see the new item.

quiz.q: Which statement about global secondary indexes is true?
options: They are updated asynchronously, so index reads are eventually consistent
They can only be created along with the table
They support strongly consistent reads
Their keys must be unique
quiz.explain: GSIs are propagated asynchronously, so a just-written item may not appear in the index yet.

concepts.name: Batch reads and writes
concepts.summary: Read up to 100 items and write up to 25 per request with BatchGetItem and BatchWriteItem, and retry unprocessed items.
concepts.why: Batching cuts round trips for bulk loads and fan-out reads, but it has rules that cause silent data loss if ignored.
concepts.body:
`BatchWriteItem` sends up to **25** put or delete requests (no updates) across one or more tables in one call; `BatchGetItem` fetches up to **100** items by full primary key. Both are capped at 16 MB per call.

A batch is **not a transaction**: each item succeeds or fails independently, and there are no conditions. When DynamoDB is throttling or partially busy, it returns the leftovers in `UnprocessedItems` (writes) or `UnprocessedKeys` (reads). You must resend those, ideally with exponential backoff. Code that ignores them loses writes without any exception.

In Python, `table.batch_writer()` handles this for you: it buffers puts and deletes, sends them in groups of 25, and retries unprocessed items automatically. `overwrite_by_pkeys=[...]` deduplicates repeated keys in the buffer (a batch may not contain the same key twice).

Batches save network round trips, not capacity: each item still costs the same read or write units as an individual call. `BatchGetItem` reads are eventually consistent unless you set `ConsistentRead` per table, and results come back in no particular order.

For loading large datasets into a new table, **Import from S3** (CSV, DynamoDB JSON or Ion) is faster and consumes no write capacity.
concepts.code:
import boto3

ddb = boto3.resource("dynamodb")
table = ddb.Table("Orders")

with table.batch_writer() as batch:          # chunks of 25, retries leftovers
    for n in range(60):
        batch.put_item(Item={"customer_id": "c7", "order_id": f"o{n:03}", "n": n})

keys = [{"customer_id": "c7", "order_id": f"o{n:03}"} for n in (1, 2, 3)]
resp = ddb.batch_get_item(RequestItems={"Orders": {"Keys": keys}})
print(sorted(int(i["n"]) for i in resp["Responses"]["Orders"]))   # [1, 2, 3]
print(resp["UnprocessedKeys"])   # {}  -> otherwise resend these
takeaways: BatchWriteItem: up to 25 puts/deletes; BatchGetItem: up to 100 gets
Batches are not atomic; retry UnprocessedItems/UnprocessedKeys
`batch_writer()` batches and retries for you
Batching saves round trips, not capacity units
pitfalls: Calling the low-level batch_write_item and never checking UnprocessedItems.

quiz.q: A BatchWriteItem call returns non-empty UnprocessedItems. What should the caller do?
options: Nothing; DynamoDB retries them later
Switch to Scan
Roll back the processed items
Resend those items, with backoff
quiz.explain: Unprocessed items were not written; the client must retry them itself.

concepts.name: Capacity modes and read consistency
concepts.summary: On-demand versus provisioned capacity, how reads and writes are metered, throttling, and eventual versus strong consistency.
concepts.why: Capacity decides your bill and your throttling behaviour; consistency decides what a read can return.
concepts.body:
DynamoDB meters work in units:

- one **read unit** = one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to **4 KB** (eventually consistent reads cost half)
- one **write unit** = one write per second of an item up to **1 KB**
- sizes round up per item: a 5 KB write costs 5 units, a 5 KB strong read costs 2
- transactional reads and writes cost double

In **on-demand** mode you pay per request and DynamoDB absorbs spikes instantly up to double the previous peak, ramping beyond that; you can set maximum throughput to cap cost. It is the recommended default. In **provisioned** mode you set RCU and WCU, usually with auto scaling; it is cheaper for steady, predictable traffic. You can switch modes.

When a request exceeds capacity, it is **throttled** with `ProvisionedThroughputExceededException` or `ThrottlingException`. The SDKs retry with backoff automatically; persistent throttling usually means a hot key rather than too little total capacity.

**Consistency**: by default `GetItem`, `Query` and `Scan` are **eventually consistent** and may miss a write from the last moment. `ConsistentRead=True` gives a strongly consistent read reflecting all successful writes, at twice the cost; it is not available on GSIs or in Streams.
concepts.code:
# Capacity arithmetic (per item, rounded up):
#
#   item 3 KB  strong read          ceil(3/4) = 1 RCU
#   item 3 KB  eventual read        0.5 RCU
#   item 9 KB  strong read          ceil(9/4) = 3 RCU
#   item 2.5 KB write               ceil(2.5/1) = 3 WCU
#   item 2.5 KB transactional write 2 * 3 = 6 WCU
#
# Query reading 40 items of 1 KB (40 KB total, strong):  40/4 = 10 RCU
# (a Query sums item sizes first, then rounds up to 4 KB)

import boto3
table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
r = table.get_item(Key={"customer_id": "c1", "order_id": "o1"},
                   ConsistentRead=True, ReturnConsumedCapacity="TOTAL")
print(r["ConsumedCapacity"])   # {'TableName': 'Orders', 'CapacityUnits': 1.0}
takeaways: Reads are metered in 4 KB, writes in 1 KB steps
Eventual reads cost half; transactions cost double
On-demand is the default choice; provisioned suits steady traffic
Strong reads cost 2x and are unavailable on GSIs
pitfalls: Storing large, rarely read attributes in frequently written items, multiplying write cost by item size.

quiz.q: How many write units does writing one 2.5 KB item cost (non-transactional)?
quiz.explain: Write units are per 1 KB rounded up, so 2.5 KB costs 3 units.

concepts.name: Designing from access patterns
concepts.summary: Model a DynamoDB table by listing access patterns first, then shaping keys, often with several entity types in one table.
concepts.why: Relational habits produce slow, expensive DynamoDB tables; access-pattern-first design is what makes it scale.
concepts.body:
Relational design starts from entities and normalizes; queries come later. DynamoDB design runs the other way:

- write down every **access pattern** with its parameters: "get user by id", "list a user's orders newest first", "get an order with its line items", "list open orders for a warehouse"
- choose keys so each pattern is a single `GetItem` or `Query` on the table or an index
- denormalize and duplicate data where it saves a read

A common technique is **single-table design**: store several entity types in one table with generic key names (`PK`, `SK`) and prefixed values. A customer and their orders share a partition, so one query fetches a customer with orders, which is DynamoDB's substitute for a join:

- customer: `PK = CUST#42`, `SK = PROFILE`
- order: `PK = CUST#42`, `SK = ORDER#2025-03-01#A17`
- line item: `PK = ORDER#A17`, `SK = ITEM#1`

Querying `PK = CUST#42` returns the profile and all orders; `begins_with(SK, "ORDER#")` returns orders only.

Single-table design is a tool, not a rule. Separate tables are fine when entities are never fetched together, and they are easier to understand, back up and stream. The goal is that every hot path is one request against a well-distributed key.
concepts.code:
import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("App")   # keys: PK (S), SK (S)
with table.batch_writer() as b:
    b.put_item(Item={"PK": "CUST#42", "SK": "PROFILE", "name": "Ann"})
    b.put_item(Item={"PK": "CUST#42", "SK": "ORDER#2025-01-09#A11", "total": 20})
    b.put_item(Item={"PK": "CUST#42", "SK": "ORDER#2025-03-01#A17", "total": 35})

# access pattern: customer with all orders, one request
both = table.query(KeyConditionExpression=Key("PK").eq("CUST#42"))["Items"]
print([i["SK"] for i in both])
# ['ORDER#2025-01-09#A11', 'ORDER#2025-03-01#A17', 'PROFILE']

# access pattern: latest order only
last = table.query(KeyConditionExpression=Key("PK").eq("CUST#42")
                   & Key("SK").begins_with("ORDER#"), ScanIndexForward=False, Limit=1)
print(last["Items"][0]["total"])   # 35
takeaways: List access patterns before choosing keys
Every hot path should be one GetItem or Query
Pre-join related items by giving them the same partition key
Prefixed generic keys (PK/SK) let one table hold many entity types
pitfalls: Normalizing into many tables and then doing several sequential reads, or scans, to assemble one screen.

quiz.q: In single-table design, how do you fetch a customer together with their orders in one request?
options: Use a JOIN in PartiQL
Give the profile and orders the same partition key and Query it
Scan with a filter on customer id
Create a transaction across two tables
quiz.explain: Items sharing a partition key form one item collection, which a single Query returns.

concepts.name: Transactions
concepts.summary: Group up to 100 actions across items and tables into an all-or-nothing TransactWriteItems or a consistent TransactGetItems.
concepts.why: Some invariants span items, such as transferring a balance or enforcing uniqueness, and need atomic multi-item writes.
concepts.body:
`TransactWriteItems` executes up to **100** actions (Put, Update, Delete, ConditionCheck) on distinct items, in one or more tables of the same account and region, **atomically**: either all succeed or none are applied. Each action can have its own condition; if any condition fails, the whole transaction is cancelled with `TransactionCanceledException`, whose `CancellationReasons` tell you which action failed. `ConditionCheck` lets you assert something about an item you do not modify.

`TransactGetItems` reads up to 100 items as a consistent snapshot.

Things to know:

- the total size limit is 4 MB, and one item cannot appear twice in a transaction
- transactional operations cost **twice** the normal capacity
- transactions conflict with concurrent writes to the same items and may be cancelled; retry them
- pass a `ClientRequestToken` to make retries **idempotent** for 10 minutes

A classic use is enforcing uniqueness of a non-key attribute: write the user item and a second item with `PK = EMAIL#ann@x.com` guarded by `attribute_not_exists`, in one transaction.

Transactions are powerful but expensive; many designs need only single-item conditional writes.
concepts.code:
import boto3

client = boto3.client("dynamodb")

def register(user_id, email):
    client.transact_write_items(TransactItems=[
        {"Put": {"TableName": "App",
                 "Item": {"PK": {"S": f"USER#{user_id}"}, "SK": {"S": "PROFILE"},
                          "email": {"S": email}},
                 "ConditionExpression": "attribute_not_exists(PK)"}},
        {"Put": {"TableName": "App",          # uniqueness marker for the email
                 "Item": {"PK": {"S": f"EMAIL#{email}"}, "SK": {"S": "EMAIL"}},
                 "ConditionExpression": "attribute_not_exists(PK)"}},
    ])

register("u1", "ann@example.com")
try:
    register("u2", "ann@example.com")    # email taken: nothing is written
except client.exceptions.TransactionCanceledException as e:
    print([r["Code"] for r in e.response["CancellationReasons"]])
    # ['None', 'ConditionalCheckFailed']
takeaways: Up to 100 actions, all-or-nothing, across tables in one region
Any failed condition cancels the whole transaction
Transactions cost double and can conflict; retry with a ClientRequestToken
Marker items plus transactions enforce uniqueness of non-key attributes
pitfalls: Using transactions for every write by default, doubling cost where a single conditional write was enough.

quiz.q: A TransactWriteItems with three Puts fails the condition on the second Put. What is written?
options: Nothing
The first and third Puts
The first Put only
All three, with a warning
quiz.explain: Transactions are atomic: one failed condition cancels every action.

concepts.name: Sparse indexes, overloading and sharding
concepts.summary: Advanced key patterns: sparse GSIs, overloaded GSI keys, inverted indexes and write sharding for hot partitions.
concepts.why: These patterns let a few indexes serve many access patterns and keep heavy traffic evenly spread.
concepts.body:
A few patterns come up in nearly every serious DynamoDB design:

- **Sparse index**: only items that have the index's key attribute are indexed. Set `open_since` only on open orders and a GSI on it lists exactly the open ones; remove the attribute when the order closes and it drops out. Small, cheap, and a natural work queue.
- **GSI overloading**: give the index generic keys (`GSI1PK`, `GSI1SK`) and let each entity type put a different meaning in them: orders by `STATUS#PENDING`, users by `EMAIL#...`. One index then serves many patterns, which matters because each GSI adds write cost.
- **Inverted index**: a GSI whose partition key is the table's sort key and vice versa, so many-to-many relationships can be read from both sides (students of a class, classes of a student).
- **Write sharding**: if one key value gets too much traffic (a global leaderboard, today's date), append a random or calculated suffix `DATE#2025-03-01#7` across N shards, and query all N shards in parallel when reading.

Also consider **composite sort keys** like `COUNTRY#STATE#CITY` so `begins_with` queries at any level work from one index.

Every pattern costs something: duplicated storage, extra writes, more complex reads. Add them for real access patterns only.
concepts.code:
import random
import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("App")   # GSI "GSI1" on (GSI1PK, GSI1SK)
SHARDS = 4

def record_vote(day, user):
    shard = random.randrange(SHARDS)               # spread one hot day over 4 keys
    table.put_item(Item={"PK": f"VOTE#{user}", "SK": day,
                         "GSI1PK": f"DAY#{day}#{shard}", "GSI1SK": user})

def votes_for(day):
    items = []
    for s in range(SHARDS):                        # read every shard
        items += table.query(IndexName="GSI1",
            KeyConditionExpression=Key("GSI1PK").eq(f"DAY#{day}#{s}"))["Items"]
    return items

for u in ["ann", "bob", "cy"]:
    record_vote("2025-03-01", u)
print(sorted(i["GSI1SK"] for i in votes_for("2025-03-01")))   # ['ann', 'bob', 'cy']
takeaways: Sparse GSIs index only items that carry the key attribute
Overloaded generic GSI keys let one index serve many patterns
Inverted indexes read many-to-many relations from both sides
Write sharding spreads a hot key; reads fan out across shards
pitfalls: Sharding a key that is not actually hot, which only multiplies read requests.

quiz.q: Why is a GSI on an attribute that only open orders have called a sparse index?
options: It stores only every tenth item
It only exists in one Availability Zone
It uses compressed storage
Items lacking the attribute are not copied into the index
quiz.explain: Index entries exist only for items that have the index key, so the index holds just the open orders.

concepts.name: Streams and TTL
concepts.summary: React to every item change with DynamoDB Streams and Lambda, and expire items automatically with Time to Live.
concepts.why: Event-driven side effects and automatic cleanup are core building blocks of serverless DynamoDB applications.
concepts.body:
**DynamoDB Streams** records every item-level change (insert, modify, remove) in order per item, retained for **24 hours**. The `StreamViewType` decides what each record carries: `KEYS_ONLY`, `NEW_IMAGE`, `OLD_IMAGE` or `NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES`.

The usual consumer is **AWS Lambda** through an event source mapping: Lambda polls the stream and invokes your function with batches of records. Use it to update aggregates, keep a search index in sync, send notifications, or replicate to another store. Records for the same item arrive in order; a function that throws will be retried with the same batch, so handlers must be **idempotent**, and you should configure a failure destination and `BisectBatchOnFunctionError` so one bad record cannot block a shard. Alternatively stream changes to **Kinesis Data Streams** for longer retention and more consumers.

**Time to Live (TTL)**: choose an attribute holding an expiry time as a **Unix epoch number in seconds**. After that time DynamoDB deletes the item in the background at no write cost, typically within a few days, not instantly. Filter out expired-but-present items in queries (`expires_at > :now`) when it matters. TTL deletions appear in the stream with a `userIdentity` of `dynamodb.amazonaws.com`, so you can archive expired items to S3.
takeaways: Streams keep 24 hours of ordered item changes; Lambda is the usual consumer
Stream handlers are retried, so make them idempotent
TTL takes an epoch-seconds number and deletes expired items for free
TTL deletion is delayed; filter expired items if exactness matters
pitfalls: Storing the TTL attribute as an ISO date string or milliseconds; TTL then never deletes the item.

quiz.q: An item's TTL attribute passed an hour ago. What can a query still return?
options: Never the item; deletion is exact to the second
An error until the item is deleted
Possibly the item, because TTL deletes in the background with a delay
Only the key attributes
quiz.explain: TTL deletion is asynchronous and can lag, so expired items may still be read until removed.

concepts.name: Partitions, hot keys and adaptive capacity
concepts.summary: How DynamoDB stores data in partitions, the per-partition throughput limits, and how adaptive capacity and splits handle heat.
concepts.why: Hot partitions are the main cause of throttling at scale, and fixing them requires knowing how data is physically placed.
concepts.body:
Internally a table is split into **partitions**, each stored on SSDs and replicated across three AZs. The partition key's hash places each item. A partition holds up to about **10 GB** and serves up to **3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second**. These limits apply per partition regardless of how much capacity the table has overall.

So a table can have plenty of total throughput and still throttle if traffic concentrates on one key, a **hot key**. DynamoDB mitigates this in several ways:

- **adaptive capacity** instantly lends unused throughput to busy partitions, up to the per-partition maximums
- **split for heat**: a partition that stays hot is split, spreading its key range across more partitions (this cannot spread a single partition key value that is itself too hot, unless the sort key range can be divided)
- partitions are added as data grows or provisioned throughput increases, and are never merged back

What this means for design: a single partition key value has a ceiling of about 1,000 writes/s, so very hot values need write sharding or caching. CloudWatch Contributor Insights shows the most accessed and throttled keys. Throttled requests in metrics such as `ThrottledRequests` with low overall consumption point to a key-distribution problem, not a capacity problem.

LSIs pin an item collection to one partition, hence their 10 GB limit.
takeaways: Each partition: about 10 GB, 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU per second
One hot partition key can throttle while the table has spare capacity
Adaptive capacity and split for heat help, but cannot fix one ultra-hot key
Use Contributor Insights to find hot keys; shard or cache them
pitfalls: Raising table capacity to cure throttling caused by a single hot key.

quiz.q: An on-demand table throttles writes while total consumption is low. Most likely cause?
options: The table is too small
Writes concentrate on one partition key beyond per-partition limits
On-demand tables cannot exceed 1,000 writes/s in total
TTL is enabled
quiz.explain: Per-partition limits apply to each key's partition, so a hot key throttles regardless of table totals.

concepts.name: Global tables and multi-Region
concepts.summary: Replicate a table across AWS Regions, understand conflict resolution and consistency choices, and plan failover.
concepts.why: Global tables give low-latency local access worldwide and Region-level resilience, but change your consistency model.
concepts.body:
A **global table** is a set of replica tables in several AWS Regions that DynamoDB keeps in sync. Every replica accepts reads and writes (**multi-active**), so users in each Region get local latency and an application can fail over by sending traffic to another Region.

With the default **multi-Region eventual consistency** (MREC), a write is acknowledged in its own Region and replicated to the others asynchronously, typically within a second. If the same item is written in two Regions concurrently, conflicts are resolved by **last writer wins** on timestamps: one write silently disappears. Designs therefore often route each item's writes to a single "home" Region, or make writes commutative.

Global tables can alternatively be configured for **multi-Region strong consistency** (MRSC), across three Regions, where a write is synchronously replicated and strongly consistent reads in any Region see the latest value, at the cost of higher write latency and some feature restrictions. Check the current docs for supported Regions and limitations.

Other points:

- conditional writes and transactions evaluate in the local Region only (transactions are not atomic across Regions under MREC)
- replicated writes consume write capacity in every Region
- TTL and streams work per replica; a TTL deletion replicates like any delete

Plan failover with Route 53 or application routing, and test it.
takeaways: Replicas in several Regions, all read/write
MREC: async replication, last writer wins on conflicts
MRSC: synchronous, strongly consistent across Regions with higher latency
Transactions and conditions are Region-local; writes are paid in every Region
pitfalls: Allowing the same item to be updated from several Regions under MREC and losing updates to last-writer-wins.

quiz.q: Under eventual-consistency global tables, two Regions update the same item at the same time. What happens?
options: The write with the later timestamp wins everywhere
Both updates are merged attribute by attribute
Both Regions roll back
The table enters a read-only state
quiz.explain: Conflicts are resolved by last writer wins, so one concurrent update is discarded.

concepts.name: Item size, caching and cost control
concepts.summary: Work within the 400 KB item limit, offload large blobs to S3, cache with DAX, and keep read and write costs predictable.
concepts.why: At scale the bill is driven by item size and request patterns, and design choices can change it by an order of magnitude.
concepts.body:
Item size multiplies cost: every write is billed per 1 KB and every read per 4 KB. Patterns that keep items lean:

- put large blobs (documents, images) in **S3** and store only the object key
- **vertical partitioning**: split a big entity into several items under one partition key (`SK = PROFILE`, `SK = SETTINGS`, `SK = HISTORY#...`) so frequent updates touch small items
- compress large text attributes (gzip into a binary attribute) when you must keep them inline
- keep attribute names short in huge tables; names count toward item size

The hard limit is **400 KB** per item, including attribute names.

**DAX** (DynamoDB Accelerator) is an in-memory, write-through cache cluster with a DynamoDB-compatible API, giving microsecond reads for read-heavy, repetitive access. It serves eventually consistent reads only and adds a cluster to run; for many apps an application-level cache or simply reading less is enough.

Other levers: use eventually consistent reads where possible (half price), project only needed attributes into GSIs, delete unused GSIs, use the **Standard-IA** table class for rarely accessed data (cheaper storage, pricier requests), switch steady workloads to provisioned capacity with auto scaling or reserved capacity, and watch `ConsumedReadCapacityUnits` per operation using `ReturnConsumedCapacity`.
concepts.code:
import gzip
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("App")
doc = ("lorem ipsum " * 4000).encode()          # ~48 KB of text

table.put_item(Item={"PK": "DOC#1", "SK": "BODY",
                     "body_gz": gzip.compress(doc)})   # binary attribute
r = table.put_item(Item={"PK": "DOC#1", "SK": "META", "title": "Notes", "views": 0},
                   ReturnConsumedCapacity="TOTAL")
print(r["ConsumedCapacity"]["CapacityUnits"])   # 1.0  small item, cheap updates

body = gzip.decompress(table.get_item(
    Key={"PK": "DOC#1", "SK": "BODY"})["Item"]["body_gz"].value)
print(len(body) // 1000, "KB raw,", len(gzip.compress(doc)), "bytes stored")
# 48 KB raw, 142 bytes stored  (repetitive text compresses well)
takeaways: Item size drives cost: writes per 1 KB, reads per 4 KB; max item 400 KB
Store blobs in S3 and split big entities into several items
DAX caches eventually consistent reads in microseconds
Eventual reads, lean GSI projections and table classes cut cost
pitfalls: Incrementing a view counter inside a 300 KB item, paying 300 write units per click.

quiz.q: A 200 KB item has a counter updated 100 times per second. What is the cheapest fix?
options: Use strongly consistent reads
Switch to Scan
Add a GSI on the counter
Move the counter into its own small item under the same partition key
quiz.explain: Each update is billed on the full item size, so a separate 1 KB item cuts write cost about 200 times.
